title: When the Postcards Wakes
premise: Noor Thornbury, a night librarian who has spent thirty years perfecting the art of not being asked questions, learns that the house on Alder Street — the one they fled at nine years old — is going to auction. Among the estate papers is a bundle of postcards their mother mailed for decades, each one a small, cheerful lie that kept a family secret buried: what happened the night Noor's father disappeared, and which sibling actually knows. As developers circle the property and the auction date closes in, Noor must decide whether to let the house and its story be sold off quietly, or claim the truth and shatter the careful arrangement of loyalties that has held three siblings together. In the end, Noor reads the final postcard aloud at the auction itself, buying nothing but ending the silence — and walks out owning only the truth, which turns out to be enough.
about_author: Vesper Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing other people's unopened letters before turning to fiction. They write at night, in libraries, about the things families keep in boxes.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. We meet Noor mid-shift at the night library, deflecting a patron's kindness with practiced ease, then returning to a bare apartment where even the books are borrowed. A letter arrives from a probate firm: the Alder Street house is entering probate auction. Emotional beat: the past arriving as paperwork, unwelcome and precise.

chapters.title: Alder Street, Third House From the Corner
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor visits the empty house under pretense of 'assessing contents' for the estate sale, walking rooms they haven't entered since childhood. In the attic they find a shoebox of postcards, all in their mother's hand, all addressed to Noor's sister Wren — none ever delivered. Emotional beat: dread disguised as nostalgia.

chapters.title: Postcards From a Woman Who Never Left
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, intercut with postcard text. The cards span twenty years, cheerful updates from a mother claiming to live in Lisbon — though she never left the city. Each card ends with the same line: 'Don't tell Tam.' Noor realizes the siblings' entire adult distance was engineered. Emotional beat: vertigo as the family's architecture reveals itself as deliberate.

chapters.title: Wren, Who Answers Doors Like Fortresses
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, a hospice nurse with immaculate boundaries, receives Noor's call and deflects. We see her privately rereading her own stack of the same postcards — she's known for years. Her loyalty to their mother's dying wish wars with guilt over letting Noor carry the blame for their father's disappearance. Emotional beat: love expressed as withholding.

chapters.title: Tam Buys Back Time
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The youngest sibling, a real-estate developer, is bidding on the Alder Street house himself — planning to demolish it before anyone can look too closely. He meets Noor there unexpectedly; old affection flickers through his sales patter. He warns them off gently, revealing he knows more than he says. Emotional beat: charm as armor over fear.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Kept
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor tracks down Mrs. Okafor, an elderly neighbor, who recalls the night the father vanished — and mentions the mother standing on the porch afterward, calm, holding a suitcase that wasn't hers. A postcard dated that same week surfaces in Okafor's own keepsakes, addressed but never sent, in the father's handwriting. Emotional beat: the ground tilting; the official story dies.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, short sections. The auction approaches; the estate lawyer releases a catalogue listing 'personal correspondence' among the lots. Wren threatens legal action; Tam offers Noor money to walk away; Noor refuses both and requests the letters be pulled — denied, sealed until sale day. Emotional beat: three siblings circling the same wound, each armed differently.

chapters.title: Lisbon, Population One
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor finally decodes the postcards' pattern: dates, stamps, and the mother's handwriting form a timeline proving the father didn't abandon them — he died that night, and the mother staged his departure to protect Tam, then a child, from something he'd witnessed. The lie wasn't cruelty; it was survival, priced across thirty years. Emotional beat: grief replacing anger.

chapters.title: Going Once
chapters.summary: All three siblings present at the auction. When lot 47 — the correspondence — comes up, Noor stands and instead of bidding, reads the final unsent postcard aloud: the mother's confession, meant for whichever child was brave enough to open the box. The room goes still; Tam drops his paddle; Wren takes Noor's hand. Emotional beat: climax — truth spoken publicly, loyalty redefined rather than destroyed.

chapters.title: Everything Not Sold
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, weeks later. The house sells to strangers; the siblings split nothing but the shoebox, each taking postcards home. Noor, still a night librarian, leaves the smile behind and lets a patron ask a question — and answers it. Final image: Noor mailing a postcard of their own, addressed to no one, telling the truth simply because it can now be told. Emotional beat: quiet, earned release.
